Sigmoid: a differentiable step

Max depth, FFN without residuals: ≈ 10 layers (quasi-linear region)
X
· Wᵀ
ŷ
σ(·)
p̂
∂L/∂p̂
p̂ = σ(ŷ) = 1 / (1 + e−ŷ)
╍ H(ŷ) for comparison
∂p̂/∂ŷ = σ(ŷ)(1 − σ(ŷ)) ≤ 0.25
positive everywhere, but small
Problem 1: the gradient shrinks. ∂p̂/∂ŷ ≤ 0.25, so every sigmoid layer cuts the back-propagated gradient by at least 4×, and by far more once |ŷ| is large.
Problem 2: the mean is not zero. σ(0) = 0.5. With weights initialised for the quasi-linear region, the mean's share of the second moment, E[p̂²] = Var[p̂] + E[p̂]², grows layer over layer.
Sigmoid fixes zero gradients but brings two new problems: shrinking gradients and a non-zero mean.
© 2026 Dr. Jesse Roberts

ReLU: a gradient of exactly 1

Max depth, FFN without residuals: ≈ 50 layers
X
· Wᵀ
ŷ
ReLU
p̂
∂L/∂p̂
p̂ = max(0, ŷ) = {
ŷ,ŷ > 0 0,ŷ ≤ 0
∂p̂/∂ŷ = {
1,ŷ > 0 0,ŷ < 0
Fixed: the gradient. ∂p̂/∂ŷ = 1 for every ŷ > 0, so active units pass the back-propagated gradient through unchanged, however many layers deep.
Still there: the non-zero mean. p̂ ≥ 0, so E[p̂] > 0, and the mean's share of E[p̂²] = Var[p̂] + E[p̂]² still grows layer over layer. That leads to correlated representations: a shared positive offset makes features move together. It also leads to dying neurons: a unit pushed to ŷ ≤ 0 for every input gets zero gradient and never recovers.
ReLU fixes the shrinking gradient but keeps the non-zero mean.
© 2026 Dr. Jesse Roberts

The scaled path carries ŷ itself, to be scaled by the gate; the composed path runs ŷ through g to decide how much. For ReLU, g = H.

ReLU′(0) taken as 0. Both are ≈ 1 on the positive side.
In later layers, correlated activations push many ReLU units below zero on every input. Those units are always off: ReLU′ = 0, so no gradient reaches their weights and they stop learning. SiLU still passes a small gradient for moderate ŷ < 0, so an off unit can recover.
SiLU keeps a small gradient where ReLU has none, so switched-off neurons can still learn.

Do we really need the nonlinear activation?

SwiGLU already multiplies two projections of the input

explicit nonlinearityproduct of two projections
x is linear. x · x is not.╍ x━ x · x
Multiplying two linear functions of the input already bends the output.
So drop the σ?
P̂ = XWᵀ ⊙ XVᵀ
p̂ₖ = (x · wₖ)(x · vₖ) = Σᵢ Σⱼ Wₖᵢ Vₖⱼ xᵢ xⱼ
x is one row of X; wₖ, vₖ are row k of W, V. Every output is a quadratic in x, built from products of input features xᵢ xⱼ. This is the bilinear layer (Mnih & Hinton, 2007; Dauphin et al., 2017).
If the product is already nonlinear, does the extra σ earn its place?
x · x is already nonlinear, so the σ in SwiGLU may be a nonlinearity we don't need.
© 2026 Dr. Jesse Roberts

Activation functions are still being invented

What we built today, one idea at a time
XWᵀ
Linear: no activation, so stacked layers collapse into one
H(XWᵀ)
Perceptron threshold: no gradient
σ(XWᵀ)
Sigmoid: differentiable, but gradient ≤ 0.25 and a non-zero mean
H(XWᵀ) ⊙ XWᵀ
ReLU: multiply by the threshold instead
σ(XWᵀ) ⊙ XWᵀ
SiLU: soften the threshold
σ(XWᵀ) ⊙ XVᵀ
GLU: gates read every feature
σ(XWᵀ) ⊙ XWᵀ ⊙ XVᵀ
SwiGLU: the current LLM default
XWᵀ ⊙ XVᵀ
Bilinear: almost as good, no σ
Open questions
Why do gated layers beat ungated ones at equal parameters?
How much of the gain is the product, and how much the σ?
What should the gate look at, and in what dimension?
Shazeer (2020), on why GLU variants work: “we attribute their success, as all else, to divine benevolence.”
Activation design is still an open research question; expect today's default to change.

SwiGLU in a feed-forward network

e = examples, din = input features, hₖ = width of layer k, o = outputs
Hₖ = σ(Hₖ₋₁Wₖᵀ) ⊙ Hₖ₋₁Wₖᵀ ⊙ Hₖ₋₁Vₖᵀ,   H₀ = x,   P̂ = softmax(H₃Woutᵀ)
Both Linears in layer k are hₖ × hₖ₋₁. With no residual stream, every layer's gradient must pass through all the layers after it.
SwiGLU drops in as the activation of a plain feed-forward network; next, we give it a residual stream.

Mixture of experts: one gate per expert

Group the hidden units into experts; a router gives each expert one gate
g = softmax(x Wrᵀ)
H = Σᵢ gᵢ · Eᵢ(x)
One gate, many units. g₁ scales both units of expert 1.
Gates compete. The softmax makes raising one gate lower the other.
In the block: P̂ ⊙ G, with gᵢ repeated over expert i's units. Shazeer et al., 2017
MoE puts one gate on a whole block of units, and the gates compete through a softmax.

Top-k routing: a hard gate on experts

Keep the k largest gates and skip the rest (here k = 1)
g̃ᵢ = gᵢ · H(gᵢ − τ)
τ = k-th largest gate
The Heaviside step is back, on whole experts. Expert 2 is never computed.
Parameters grow with E; compute with k. Huge but sparse: Kimi K2 uses ≈ 3% of its weights per token.

Keeping every expert in use

A skipped expert gets no gradient, so routing can collapse onto a few experts
L = Ltask + α · N · Σᵢ fᵢ Pᵢ
fᵢ: fraction of tokens sent to expert i (a count, no gradient)
Pᵢ: mean router probability for expert i (has a gradient)
Smallest when every fᵢ = Pᵢ = 1/N; α = 0.01.
This term balances load. The sparsity still comes from top-k.
The extra loss term balances load across experts; top-k supplies the sparsity.
